Probabilistic Deep Learning: Distributional Heads, MC Dropout, and Deep Ensembles

Source: vignettes/v13-probabilistic-deep-learning.qmd

Package: sciModelFlowR
Version targeted: 0.6.0
Status: source-complete; runtime validation deferred to the consolidated local validation cycle.

The code blocks are designed for local execution after optional Deep Learning backends are installed. The package does not require torch, luz, or keras3 merely to load the core scientific workflow.

1 1. Why uncertainty needs a typed source

Version 0.6.0 does not create a generic uncertainty number. It records how uncertainty was generated and what it conditions on.

2 2. Learning objectives

After this vignette, the reader should be able to create a distributional head, validate its constraints, fit Gaussian-output regression, use MC dropout and deep ensembles, separate aleatoric and epistemic components only when identifiable, and evaluate uncertainty with probabilistic scores.

3 3. Gold nonlinear heteroscedastic fixture 

d <- smf_load_dataset("gold_dl_nonlinear")
head(d)

truth_mu and truth_sigma are validation-only generator quantities.

4 4. Gaussian distributional head 

base <- smf_mlp(
  input_dim = 6,
  output_dim = 1,
  hidden = c(128, 64),
  dropout = 0.10,
  task = "regression"
)

gaussian <- smf_dl_distributional_head(
  base,
  distribution = "normal"
)

gaussian

Internally the network emits location and log-scale parameters. The log-scale parameterization avoids unconstrained negative standard deviations.

5 5. Train the distributional model 

spec <- smf_dl_spec(
  gaussian,
  epochs = 100,
  batch_size = 32,
  device = "cpu",
  patience = 12,
  parameters = list(learning_rate = 1e-3)
)

# fit <- smf_dl_train(
#   d,
#   "y",
#   gaussian,
#   spec,
#   predictors = paste0("x", 1:6),
#   task = "regression"
# )

6 6. PredictionDistribution

A Gaussian head is converted to the common PredictionDistribution contract so downstream scoring does not depend on torch.

7 7. Aleatoric uncertainty

Conditional scale from the distributional head is an aleatoric component under the assumed Gaussian family. It should be checked against residual patterns and empirical interval coverage.

8 8. MC dropout 

# mc <- smf_dl_mc_dropout(
#   fit,
#   new_data = d[1:50, ],
#   draws = 200,
#   seed = 260915
# )

Dropout probability must be greater than zero. The package does not call a deterministic network “MC dropout”.

9 9. Deep ensembles 

# ens <- smf_dl_ensemble(
#   d,
#   target = "y",
#   architecture = gaussian,
#   spec = spec,
#   predictors = paste0("x", 1:6),
#   task = "regression",
#   members = 5,
#   seeds = 260915:260919
# )
#
# ep <- smf_dl_predict_distribution(ens, as.matrix(d[1:50, ]), method = "ensemble")

Each seed is stored separately. Duplicate seeds are rejected.

10 10. Decomposition with a Gaussian ensemble

For member (m), let (_m(x)) and (_m^2(x)) be the predicted Gaussian parameters. The package can summarize:

  • aleatoric component: mean of (_m^2(x));
  • epistemic approximation: variance of (_m(x)) across members;
  • total: their sum.

This is a model-based decomposition, not a universal partition of uncertainty.

11 11. Prediction intervals 

# smf_dl_interval(ep@uncertainty, level = 0.90)

Empirical coverage must be assessed on held-out data.

12 12. Classification probabilities

Binary and multiclass outputs use sigmoid or softmax representations. Ensemble dispersion of class probabilities is reported as an approximation to between-model uncertainty.

13 13. Calibration after neural prediction

Use the calibration layer from 0.3.0 on a separate calibration set. Do not fit a calibrator on the final test set.

14 14. Probabilistic scores

Relevant criteria include:

  • negative log likelihood;
  • Brier score for class probability;
  • CRPS for continuous predictive distributions;
  • interval score;
  • empirical coverage;
  • mean interval width;
  • calibration error.

15 15. Sharpness versus calibration

A narrow interval is useful only if coverage is adequate. Very wide intervals can obtain high coverage while offering little decision value.

16 16. MC dropout limitations

MC dropout depends on where dropout is placed, its probability, and how the network was trained. It is not automatically a Bayesian posterior.

17 17. Ensemble limitations

Ensembles can underestimate structural uncertainty when all members share the same architecture, preprocessing, loss and training data.

18 18. Distributional misspecification

A Gaussian head can be poorly calibrated for skewed, heavy-tailed or multimodal outcomes even if mean prediction is accurate.

19 19. Heteroscedasticity validation

The Gold fixture provides truth_sigma. During local validation, assess rank correlation and calibration between predicted and generator scale without using truth_sigma as an input.

20 20. Resampling and probabilistic DL

Outer resampling remains the correct level for generalization estimates. Inner validation controls training. These are distinct.

21 21. Multiple seeds

If performance varies materially by seed, report that variation. Selecting only the best seed turns initialization into an unreported tuning parameter.

22 22. Decision analysis

Probabilistic predictions become useful when connected to a decision rule: probability of failure, expected loss, probability of exceeding an agronomic threshold, or interval-based risk.

23 23. Common mistakes

  • calling softmax output “uncertainty”;
  • conflating ensemble variance with total predictive uncertainty;
  • using the same data for early stopping, calibration and final evaluation;
  • hiding failed ensemble members;
  • selecting the seed with the best test score;
  • reporting interval width without coverage.

24 24. Minimum reporting checklist

Document head distribution, likelihood/loss, ensemble or dropout settings, number and identity of seeds, number of stochastic draws, calibration method, held-out scoring rule, empirical coverage and the exact uncertainty decomposition used.

25 25. Integrated probabilistic workflow 

d <- smf_load_dataset("gold_dl_nonlinear")
x <- paste0("x", 1:6)

arch <- smf_dl_distributional_head(
  smf_mlp(6, 1, hidden = c(64, 32), dropout = .15),
  "normal"
)

spec <- smf_dl_spec(
  arch,
  epochs = 80,
  patience = 10,
  device = "cpu",
  parameters = list(learning_rate = .002)
)

# fit <- smf_dl_train(d, "y", arch, spec, predictors = x)
# mc  <- smf_dl_mc_dropout(fit, d[1:100, ], draws = 200)

26 26. Final perspective

A probabilistic network is useful when its distributional output is calibrated for the scientific decision, not merely because it emits more numbers than a point predictor.

26.0.1 Scientific interpretation note

A probabilistic neural network should be evaluated as a probabilistic model, not merely by RMSE or accuracy. Distributional heads make parameters of a predictive distribution outputs of the network. For a Gaussian regression head, for example, the network predicts a location and a scale. The scale must remain positive, and its scientific interpretation is conditional on the assumed distributional family and on the information supplied to the network.

26.0.2 Scientific interpretation note

MC dropout and deep ensembles represent different approximations. MC dropout samples predictions under stochastic dropout masks for one fitted parameter set. A deep ensemble fits multiple networks from independently recorded seeds, allowing training dynamics and local optima to vary. Neither is a literal posterior distribution. sciModelFlowR therefore labels the source of uncertainty rather than presenting all predictive samples under a generic ‘Bayesian’ heading.

26.0.3 Scientific interpretation note

Aleatoric and epistemic components are separated only when the model supports the decomposition. A Gaussian distributional head can supply a conditional variance, while variation among ensemble members or MC-dropout draws can provide an approximation to model uncertainty. The package uses the law of total variance only under that structure. If a point-output ensemble is fitted, the between-member component can be reported, but an aleatoric component is not invented.

26.0.4 Scientific interpretation note

Calibration remains necessary after a neural network produces probabilities. Softmax confidence is not automatically a calibrated probability. The calibration machinery introduced in 0.3.0 remains applicable, provided calibration data are separated from the final test set. Probabilistic DL therefore reuses the same scoring vocabulary: log score, Brier score, CRPS where appropriate, interval score, empirical coverage, sharpness, and calibration diagnostics.

A probabilistic neural network should be evaluated as a probabilistic model, not merely by RMSE or accuracy. Distributional heads make parameters of a predictive distribution outputs of the network. For a Gaussian regression head, for example, the network predicts a location and a scale. The scale must remain positive, and its scientific interpretation is conditional on the assumed distributional family and on the information supplied to the network.

26.0.66 Scientific interpretation note

MC dropout and deep ensembles represent different approximations. MC dropout samples predictions under stochastic dropout masks for one fitted parameter set. A deep ensemble fits multiple networks from independently recorded seeds, allowing training dynamics and local optima to vary. Neither is a literal posterior distribution. sciModelFlowR therefore labels the source of uncertainty rather than presenting all predictive samples under a generic ‘Bayesian’ heading.

26.0.67 Scientific interpretation note

Aleatoric and epistemic components are separated only when the model supports the decomposition. A Gaussian distributional head can supply a conditional variance, while variation among ensemble members or MC-dropout draws can provide an approximation to model uncertainty. The package uses the law of total variance only under that structure. If a point-output ensemble is fitted, the between-member component can be reported, but an aleatoric component is not invented.

26.0.68 Scientific interpretation note

Calibration remains necessary after a neural network produces probabilities. Softmax confidence is not automatically a calibrated probability. The calibration machinery introduced in 0.3.0 remains applicable, provided calibration data are separated from the final test set. Probabilistic DL therefore reuses the same scoring vocabulary: log score, Brier score, CRPS where appropriate, interval score, empirical coverage, sharpness, and calibration diagnostics.
